title: Find the Running Median
directAnswer: Maintain two heaps: a MAX-heap `lower` holding the smaller half and a MIN-heap `upper` holding the larger half. Each new value goes to a half, then you rebalance so their sizes differ by at most one. The median is the top of `lower` when it has the extra element, or the average of both tops when sizes are equal. Each insertion is O(log n); printing after each gives O(n log n) total and O(1) median lookup.

remember.pattern: Two heaps straddling the median (max-heap lower half, min-heap upper half)
remember.formula:
if lower empty or x <= lower.top: lower.push(x)   # max-heap
else: upper.push(x)                                  # min-heap
rebalance so |len(lower) - len(upper)| <= 1, lower never smaller
median = lower.top                if len(lower) > len(upper)
       = (lower.top + upper.top)/2 if equal
rules: `lower` is a **max-heap** (its top is the largest of the small half); `upper` is a **min-heap** (its top is the smallest of the large half). The median sits between the two tops.
Keep the invariant `len(lower) == len(upper)` or `len(lower) == len(upper) + 1` — let `lower` hold the extra element on odd counts.
Rebalance **every** insertion: if one heap gets 2 ahead, move its top to the other heap.
Median is **`lower.top`** on odd count, **`(lower.top + upper.top) / 2.0`** on even count — use floating division and print one decimal.
In Java use `PriorityQueue` with `Collections.reverseOrder()` for the max-heap; in Python negate values for the max-heap since `heapq` is a min-heap only.
whenToUse: Median (or any percentile near the middle) of a growing stream
Repeated 'middle element' queries while elements keep arriving
Balancing two halves so both extremes are O(1) to read
antiSignals: Whole array is known upfront and you query the median once → nth_element / quickselect in O(n)
You need arbitrary order statistics, not just the median → an order-statistics BST / Fenwick tree
Values are bounded small integers → a counting/Fenwick approach can give O(log range)
remember.takeaway: Two heaps keep a stream split at the median so both middle elements are always one peek away. 'Balance two heaps around a pivot quantity' is the go-to streaming-statistic pattern.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you reach for two heaps to get O(log n) insertion with O(1) median, and whether you get the rebalancing invariant and even/odd median formula exactly right.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Letting the heap sizes drift apart, reading the wrong heap's top, integer-dividing the even-case median (losing the .5), or mixing up which heap is max vs min.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the size invariant precisely, explain why the two tops bracket the median, and mention the language-specific max-heap trick (reverseOrder in Java, negation in Python).

problemStatement:
Numbers arrive one at a time. After reading each number, print the median of all numbers seen so far.

If the count of numbers seen is odd, the median is the middle element of the sorted sequence. If it is even, the median is the average of the two middle elements.

Print each median on its own line, formatted to one decimal place.
constraints: Print each running median to exactly one decimal place
Median of an even count is the average of the two middle values (may end in .5)
understanding: We need the median after every insertion, not just at the end, and elements keep coming. Re-sorting each time is O(n log n) per step. The efficient idea is to keep the sequence split into a smaller half and a larger half so the median is always at the boundary — and a heap gives O(1) access to the boundary element of each half.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I report the median after every insertion or only once?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: After every insertion — that's why an incremental structure (two heaps) beats re-sorting.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How is the even-count median defined?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The average of the two middle elements, so it can be a .5 value — use floating-point division.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What output format is expected?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Each median on its own line, formatted to one decimal place (e.g. 8.0, 4.5).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can numbers repeat or be zero?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Duplicates and zeros are ordinary values; the comparison with the max-heap top still routes them correctly.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Insert into a Sorted List
approaches.whenToMention: State first to frame the cost; it's the obvious incremental idea before heaps.
hints: If you kept the numbers seen so far in sorted order, where is the median?
Maintain a sorted list. Insert each new value in its correct position (binary search to find it, but the shift is the costly part).
Median is then the middle element (or average of the two middle) — O(1) to read, but each insertion shifts elements in O(n).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Binary search finds the insertion point in O(log n), but inserting into an array shifts up to n elements → O(n) per insertion, O(n²) over the whole stream. Median lookup itself is O(1).
approaches.explanation:
Keep a list of all values seen so far in sorted order. For each new value, binary-search its insertion index and insert it there, then read the median from the middle position(s).

**Why it's the natural first idea.** It directly mirrors the definition — 'the median is the middle of the sorted values' — and gives O(1) median reads once the list is maintained.

**Why it's too slow.** Although finding the position is O(log n), physically inserting into a contiguous list shifts every element after it, costing O(n) per step and O(n²) overall. For n = 10⁵ that's ~10¹⁰ shifts — too slow. A balanced BST or skip list would make insertion O(log n), but that's more machinery than the two-heap trick, which needs no ordering of the whole sequence — only the boundary.
approaches.insight: We don't actually need the entire sequence sorted — we only need the one or two elements at the median boundary. Maintaining full sorted order is overkill; two heaps maintain just the boundary in O(log n).

dryRun.intro: Keep a sorted list; read the middle after each insert.

java.explanation: Find the insertion index in O(log n); negative result encodes where it would go.
The O(n) part — inserting shifts every later element.
Even count → average the two middle elements with floating division.

python.explanation: Binary-search insertion; the underlying list shift is O(n).
Even count → average of the two middles; /2.0 keeps the .5.

Assuming binary search makes insertion O(log n) — the array shift is still O(n).

approaches.name: Two Heaps — Max-Heap + Min-Heap (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The expected answer — describe it as 'split the stream at the median with a max-heap and a min-heap'.
hints: You only ever need the element(s) at the median boundary, not the whole sorted order. What structure gives O(1) access to the largest of a set, or the smallest?
Use a max-heap `lower` for the smaller half and a min-heap `upper` for the larger half. New value: if it's ≤ lower's top, it belongs in the lower half, else the upper.
After inserting, if the heaps' sizes differ by more than one, move the top of the bigger heap to the other. Median = lower.top (odd) or average of both tops (even).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each insertion does O(1) heap peeks and at most a constant number of O(log n) pushes/pops (insert + one rebalance move), so O(log n) per element and O(n log n) for the stream. The two heaps store all n elements → O(n) space. Median read is O(1).
approaches.explanation:
Split the numbers into a smaller half (`lower`, a **max-heap**) and a larger half (`upper`, a **min-heap**). The largest of the small half (`lower.top`) and the smallest of the large half (`upper.top`) straddle the median.

**Routing a new value.** If `lower` is empty or `x <= lower.top`, `x` belongs in the small half → push to `lower`; otherwise push to `upper`. This keeps every element in `lower` ≤ every element in `upper`.

**Rebalancing.** After the push, one heap may be two elements ahead. Restore the invariant `len(lower) == len(upper)` or `len(lower) == len(upper) + 1`: if `lower` is more than one ahead, pop its max and push onto `upper`; if `upper` is ahead at all, pop its min and push onto `lower`. We deliberately let `lower` carry the extra element on odd counts so the odd-median is simply `lower.top`.

**Reading the median.** If the counts are equal, the two middle elements are exactly the two tops, so the median is `(lower.top + upper.top) / 2.0`. If `lower` has one more, the single middle element is `lower.top`. Both are O(1).

**Why two heaps beat a sorted list.** A heap gives O(1) access to just the boundary element we need and O(log n) insertion, instead of paying O(n) to keep the whole sequence ordered. We never need the full order — only the median boundary.

**Language notes.** Java's `PriorityQueue` is a min-heap; build the max-heap with `new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder())`. Python's `heapq` is min-only, so implement the max-heap by pushing negated values and negating on peek.
approaches.insight: The median is a moving boundary; two heaps keep that boundary materialised as their tops at all times. The general technique — 'maintain two balanced heaps around a pivot statistic' — also solves Sliding Window Median and IPO/most-profit scheduling.

dryRun.intro: lower = max-heap (small half), upper = min-heap (large half). Rebalance so lower never trails and leads by at most 1.

5 > 4 → upper; upper ahead → move 5 to lower
3 <= 5 → lower; lower 2 ahead → move 5 to upper

java.explanation: Max-heap for the small half — Java's default PQ is a min-heap, so reverseOrder flips it.
Route x to the small half when it's not greater than the current small-half maximum.
lower leads by 2 → shift its max to upper to restore balance.
Equal sizes → the two tops are the two middles; /2.0 keeps the .5.
Odd count → lower holds the extra element, so its top IS the median.

python.explanation: -lower[0] is the real max of the small half (values are stored negated).
Negate on push to simulate a max-heap with Python's min-heap.
Pop lower's max (un-negate) and move it to upper when lower leads by 2.
Average the two tops (un-negating lower's) for the even case.

diagrams.title: Heaps balanced around the median
diagrams.caption: lower (max-heap) and upper (min-heap); tops bracket the median.

pitfalls: Letting heap sizes drift apart — rebalance after every insertion.
Reading the wrong heap's top, or averaging when the count is odd.
Integer division on the even-case median — must use 2.0 / float.
Forgetting Python's heapq is min-only — negate values for the max-heap.
Comparing x to the wrong heap when routing (compare to lower's max).

edgeCases.behavior: Duplicates route into lower (x <= top) and rebalance → medians 5.0, 5.0, 5.0.
lower empty → push 0; odd count → median 0.0 (zero is a valid value).

commonMistakes: Failing to rebalance after every insertion, letting one heap grow unbounded.
Using integer division for the even-count median and losing the .5.
Reading the top of the wrong heap (or averaging on an odd count).
Forgetting that Python's heapq is a min-heap and not negating for the max-heap.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Integer division on the even median
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Averaging the two middle values with integer division truncates: (4 + 5) / 2 = 4 instead of 4.5.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Not negating for Python's max-heap
commonMistakesDetailed.why: heapq is min-only. Pushing raw values makes `lower` a min-heap, so lower[0] is the smallest of the small half — the routing comparison and median are then wrong.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
heapq.heappush(lower, x)
# ... compare x <= lower[0]  (lower[0] is the MIN, not the max)
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
heapq.heappush(lower, -x)
# ... compare x <= -lower[0]  (-lower[0] is the true max)
